# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. It is caused by the extracellular deposition of amyloid fibrils in the myocardium and in the majority of cases occurs due to transthyretin (ATTR) or immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloidosis. [1] Historically regarded as rare, cardiac amyloidosis—particularly the transthyretin (ATTR) form—is increasingly recognized as an underdiagnosed cause of heart failure. In a landmark prospective study, consecutive patients ≥60 years admitted with HFpEF and left ventricular hypertrophy ≥12 mm underwent ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD scintigraphy, and 16 of 120 (13.3%) showed moderate-to-severe cardiac uptake [2]. Systematic community screening has confirmed this burden, showing that although only 1.3% of patients had clinically recognized ATTR-CM, systematic screening with technetium Tc 99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy identified ATTR-CM in 6.3% of patients [3]. ATTR arises either from inherited *TTR* gene variants (ATTRv) or with aging (wild-type, ATTRwt). ATTRv often present with a heterogeneous mix of cardiac or neurologic manifestations, whereas patients with ATTRwt have predominantly cardiac manifestations. [4]

## Pathophysiology

Both major subtypes share a final common pathway of fibril deposition but differ in precursor protein. AL amyloidosis is a lethal form of systemic amyloidosis arising from clonal expansion of CD38+ plasma cells that produce misfolded immunoglobulin light chains, which form amyloid fibrils deposited in tissues. [5] In ATTR, transthyretin is a thyroxine transport protein predominantly produced by the liver, and more than 100 different mutations destabilize its tetrameric structure, promoting TTR dissociation and misassembly into oligomeric aggregates including amyloid fibrils. [6] Tetramer dissociation into monomers is the rate-limiting amyloidogenic step, a concept central to the kinetic-stabilizer therapeutic strategy [7].

## Diagnosis

A central advance has been the development of noninvasive diagnostic criteria. The combined findings of grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on bone scintigraphy and the absence of a monoclonal protein in serum or urine had a specificity and positive predictive value for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis of 100%, enabling diagnosis without histology in patients without a monoclonal gammopathy. [8] Critically, exclusion of a plasma cell clone is mandatory because more than 20% of patients with AL cardiac amyloidosis will have grade 2 or 3 radiotracer uptake [9]; an abnormal scan with monoclonal protein still requires biopsy. Cardiac magnetic resonance contributes both diagnostically and prognostically: CMR with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is a reference standard for the diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis. [10] In a large cohort, LGE was classified into none, subendocardial, and transmural patterns, which were associated with increasing amyloid burden as defined by extracellular volume. [11]

## Prognosis and Staging

Cardiac involvement dominates prognosis in AL amyloidosis, prompting biomarker-based staging. The revised Mayo system showed that FLC-diff, cTnT, and NT-proBNP were independently prognostic for overall survival, with patients assigned a score of 1 for each of FLC-diff ≥18 mg/dL, cTnT ≥0.025 ng/mL, and NT-proBNP ≥1,800 pg/mL, creating stages I to IV. [12] An analogous biomarker-based staging system was developed for ATTRwt cardiac amyloidosis [13]. Without disease-modifying therapy, prognosis is poor, with reported 5-year mortality of nearly 60% and an even worse outlook for AL [1].

## Treatment of ATTR Cardiomyopathy

The therapeutic landscape has been transformed by TTR stabilizers and gene-silencing agents. In the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial, tafamidis was studied in patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (N Engl J Med 2018;379:1007-1016), and tafamidis resulted in a 13.4% absolute reduction in overall mortality and a 22% absolute reduction in yearly cardiovascular hospitalization at 30 months compared to placebo. [14] Acoramidis, a high-affinity stabilizer, was subsequently evaluated in ATTRibute-CM: acoramidis was superior to placebo, achieving a statistically significant primary endpoint by a hierarchical win ratio analysis of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular hospitalizations, NT-proBNP, and 6-minute walk distance (win ratio 1.8; P<0.001). [15] The repurposed NSAID diflunisal also stabilizes TTR; a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agent, it stabilizes transthyretin tetramers and prevents amyloid fibril formation in vitro, and slowed polyneuropathy progression in a randomized trial [16].

Gene-silencing therapies represent a complementary mechanism. Patisiran, an RNA interference therapeutic that inhibits hepatic transthyretin production, was assigned in a phase 3 trial to patients with hereditary or wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis. [17] In APOLLO-B, treatment with patisiran over 12 months preserved functional capacity, health status, and quality of life. [18] The siRNA agent vutrisiran provided mortality benefit in HELIOS-B: vutrisiran reduced all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events (HR 0.72; P=0.01) [19], and was published as Vutrisiran in Patients with Transthyretin Amyloidosis with Cardiomyopathy (N Engl J Med 2025;392:33-44) [20]. An investigational antibody, NI006, targets amyloid removal: ATTR cardiomyopathy is a progressive and fatal disease caused by misfolded transthyretin, and despite advances in slowing progression, there has been no available treatment that depletes existing amyloid. [21]

## Treatment of AL Amyloidosis

AL therapy targets the clonal plasma cells. In the ANDROMEDA trial, patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis received six cycles of bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone either alone or with subcutaneous daratumumab followed by single-agent daratumumab. [22] The addition of daratumumab resulted in significantly higher hematologic complete response (53%) and VGPR rates (78%) compared to VCd, leading to D-VCd becoming the accepted frontline therapy. [23] Achievement of deep hematologic response is associated with improved organ responses and survival [24]. Comprehensive multidisciplinary care frameworks, such as the 2023 ACC expert consensus decision pathway on comprehensive multidisciplinary care for the patient with cardiac amyloidosis (J Am Coll Cardiol 2023;81:1076-1126), now guide management [25].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from an untreatable rarity to a recognized and increasingly manageable disease. Heightened clinical suspicion, noninvasive scintigraphy, and CMR enable earlier diagnosis [8,10,26], while contemporary cohorts demonstrate that earlier diagnosis improves outcomes over the course of 20 years [27]. Real-world data confirm that early diagnosis and treatment with tafamidis are important, with real-world survival exceeding ATTR-ACT and supporting tafamidis safety and effectiveness [28]. The expanding pharmacologic armamentarium of stabilizers [15], silencers [19,20], and emerging amyloid-depleting antibodies [21], coupled with effective plasma cell–directed regimens in AL [23], offers genuine hope; biomarker staging [12,13] and structured care pathways [25] remain essential to optimizing patient selection and outcomes [29,30].
